title: Pensieve Discuss: Scalable Small-Group CS Tutoring System with AI
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing effective small-group tutoring in large computer science courses while maintaining collaboration and timely support. The authors ask whether an AI-powered system can help scale tutoring sessions by combining shared workspaces, automated feedback, and human TA oversight.

The intervention is Pensieve Discuss, a platform for small-group CS problem solving that includes a synchronized code editor, an AI tutor powered by GPT-4, an autograder, and TA monitoring/feedback tools. The system was deployed in a CS1 course at a public university, first in a short pilot to 150 students and then for an entire Spring 2024 semester with about 800 students. Students worked in groups of up to seven during 80-minute in-person discussion sections, with either in-person or remote TAs supervising multiple groups.

The study used student surveys, usage logs, and TA interviews to examine collaboration, perceived AI helpfulness, satisfaction, and chat usage. The results suggest that Pensieve Discuss increased reported collaboration and student satisfaction relative to the previous non-AI, non-synced editor setup, and also increased the volume of questions asked. Students generally rated the AI tutor as helpful, while TAs reported that it was usually correct but sometimes overly complex. The authors conclude that AI-supported small-group tutoring is a promising direction for scaling CS instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systems/deployment study using surveys, usage logs, and a small number of TA interviews, but it is not a randomized or tightly controlled causal evaluation. Comparisons are mainly across semesters with acknowledged confounds (e.g. different student populations and slight problem differences).
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive associations and strong user preference, but the evidence for learning impact is indirect and not based on achievement outcomes. The observed effects are mostly modest-to-unclear for educational impact despite clear operational and experience benefits.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-powered AI tutor for real-time small-group CS1 discussion sections, answering student questions with hints and scaffolded guidance while avoiding giving direct solutions; integrated alongside human TA oversight and synced group chat.
Synced collaborative code editor and autograder used for scaffolded fill-in-the-blank programming problems during small-group tutoring sessions.

finding.finding_summary: The system increased collaboration in small-group CS tutoring sessions. Student survey ratings of collaboration were consistently higher in the semester using Pensieve Discuss than in the prior semester without it, and collaboration was positively correlated with satisfaction (r=0.51).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of collaboration; correlation with satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: Students reported higher satisfaction with the discussion experience when using Pensieve Discuss compared with the previous non-synced editor interface. In the pilot comparison, 77.8% preferred the new system, and 32% strongly preferred it; satisfaction was also positively correlated with collaboration (r=0.51) and AI helpfulness (r=0.30).
finding.measure: Student satisfaction survey and system preference ratings
finding.study_size: n=800 semester deployment; pilot comparison n=150

finding.finding_summary: The platform substantially increased question volume during discussion sections. TAs reported that students asked about 5.87 questions per group per section through the platform (~0.84 per student), compared with about 12.5 total questions in a 30-student section previously (~0.42 per student), suggesting roughly a doubling of question rate.
finding.measure: Chat/question volume per group per section

finding.finding_summary: The TA dashboard improved instructors’ ability to monitor student progress in real time across multiple groups, but usage of the TA-student chat channel remained low. TAs reported the view helped them understand group progress better than prior semesters, while only 61 of 1314 sessions (4.6%) included TA-sent chat messages.
finding.measure: TA interview reports; TA chat usage logs
